top_comments: This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

Longtime 1Password user here who maintains a local-only vault (and is therefore stuck on older versions of their apps/extensions) out of concern for incidents like this.I've read their architecture docs about why online vaults are safe, and I understand that they have more resources to throw at securing infrastructure than I do. But "malicious actor pushes code to production services" seems like exactly the foundation for someone to eventually insert themselves into the middle of a user's access to decrypted vault contents.I really wish 1Password would return to supporting local-only vaults.

> push malicious code to backend servicesThis is a huge red flag, and was not addressed sufficiently in this announcement.Do they not disable push to main? I don’t see this addressed in the action items or elsewhere in the writeup, whether they were missing branch protection rules or whether these were able to be bypassed.

articles.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
articles.summary: See also The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths [pdf] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50637220

top_comments: My serious opinion, is that as humans:(1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off.(2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening.(3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit.This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life.The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide.Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg.Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter.What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

AI is good at analytic a priori things like axiomatic math and that's good, but it doesn't follow that it will write the Encyclopedia Galactica or "solve" other fields, much less that it will play the sci-fi role and kills us all. It might; it might not. It just doesn't follow from a bunch of math proofs.I think mathies are really wedded to the notion that they are the queen of the sciences, and I even agree with that, but the entire corpus of "science" before and up to the start of the scientific revolution was based on notion that it would be like Euclid. Major philosophers of the three major Abrahamic faiths wrote works along those lines. And so people like Galileo were considered cranks because they violated the axioms of that kind of system. People didn't even believe in non-Euclidean geometry at all until ~200 ya.But it's not true. There's more to reality than that kind of system. I'm not saying it cannot do it one day, but Aarsonson is more or less thinking we're in the singularity because his field has been solved and really showed his hand in a reply to a troll comment. Yes, it's glib to ask "what's all this for" and, again, I love math, I find math beautiful, and I have studied a lot of it.But even a major break in some of our crypto systems isn't the singularity. It's sort of like Y2K all over again.The world ending because my job has been replaced is even a meme, it's just happening to people with credentials and a large vocabulary now.

articles.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
articles.summary: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic

top_comments: Nice! The more readable 300kloc proof even has a clear "known math" vs "new math" split and human-readable documentation all over the place. This should greatly aid with digesting it.
From ~17M lines to just ~76k lines, a 99.56% reduction.
Zulip discussion here: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/658556-Riem...

I don't think it is this particular model - after training a LoRa on Qwen 35B-A3B for typed decisions myself, it performs better than Jev at some specific tasks that require inbuilt knowledge, despite losing the overall benchmark; unless they removed some layers that would not be possible.

"Latency doesn't lie" but your data shows that you just looking at latency can't distinguish between Qwen and Gemma. Not totally convinced by this data. Self identification is the interesting part but we don't get the self-identification experiment data run on other decision models.

TypeSafe's website explicitly denies it being an LLM:>Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.so think we're going to need something far more conclusive here to conclude it is an LLM let alone a specific one.I'm also surprised anyone is still trying to identify LLMs by asking it what it is. That's been known to be wildly unreliable since the earliest days of chatgpt.Personally I think we're dealing with something closer to a neural net that was trained with LLM guidance - like for example qwen.

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

top_comments: Vanishingly few people _enjoy_ encountering generative AI in images or sounds in the wild. The most likely positive sentiment you’ll find is some version of “I don’t have an opinion”, but enough people loathe it that willingly using it or being connected to it is a liability. NYT’s position is similar to Tidal banning it from their platform this past week. This linked article references the social stigma associated with using it, which anecdotally I’m seeing daily not only in the music spaces I occupy but in ultra-normy haunts: my neighborhood subreddit, Q/A events at my kid’s school, social media posts from accounts that are typically apolitical. The disconnect between various orgs’ and industries’ drive to integrate gen AI into professional creative software and consumer sentiment is fascinating and will be something we study for a long time.

I work in the creative tools space.This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image.Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility.Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

With the competition moving to single payment and you own the software for life, subscription is finally dying.Microsoft also is pushing companies to Linux and LibreOffice suite which requires no subscription, and works just as good if not better.All we need is big names such as NYT to make the move, the rest will follow. Europe is already running away from USA software companies, now it is just a matter of time.

articles.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs
articles.summary: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs

top_comments: While the effort is interesting, I found two issues in the list.First, (.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2) fails because byte arrays store bytes and the argument 2 to `.indexOf` is a Long value. Simple type checking (via eyeballing) could have flagged the incorrect usage. I think such exercises can be more helpful if we can reduce the noise.Second, (get "abc" 1.9) fails because `get` coerces the given key to integer in the context of string objects, which makes sense; specifically in the context of weakly typed language. That said, I believe that detailed documentation of the behavior of `get` can help clients just as well as returning `nil` or not-found value. However, we are still left with questions such as "who and where do we draw the line about the dynamism of the language?" and "what is the agreed upon semantics that we are checking against?"

So this kind of work is done in Lean now, too? Based on a glimpse into the world of dependently typed languages in the 2010s, I assumed Rocq (formerly Coq) was used to verify program correctness.Are language models significantly better at writing Lean than Rocq?

That is interesting, given heavy hitters like Nubank (Brazilian digital bank) basically runs on Clojure, having bought / acquihired Rich's Cognitect. I would normally expect such primitive types and functions to be spotless.

From the stable kernel maintainer (2025):> Along the lines of the huge number of recorded CVEs, you HAVE to take all of the stable/LTS releases in order to have a secure and stable system. If you attempt to cherry-pick random patches you will NOT fix all of the known, and unknown, problems, but rather you will end up with a potentially more insecure system, and one that contains known bugs. Reliance on an "enterprise" distribution to provide this for your systems is up to you, discuss it with them as to how they achieve this result as this is what you are paying for. If you aren't paying for it, just use Debian, they know what they are doing and track the stable kernels and have a larger installed base than any other Linux distro.https://social.kernel.org/objects/56a20bd3-d2c3-4262-8388-3a...

At $DAYJOB we’ve moved all of our server images to Debian from Ubuntu because of this. It’s absolutely unacceptable for one of the most widely-used Linux distros to have slow security response times in 2026.

Please keep in mind that most major distros spend a lot of time on regression testing.While distros like Debian do an absolutely fantastic job, they have little resources for QA and regressions like this can happen: https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=1154101
